title: Price and value
subtitle: Where the money goes
objectives: Explain how a bottle's price is built
Explain why cheap wine has little wine value

steps.title: Building a price
steps.body: A bottle's price includes grapes, winemaking, packaging, transport, duty, tax, and the margins of each seller. In the UK, duty on a 750 ml bottle at 11 to 14.5% was about 2.67 pounds in 2023, plus 20% VAT. On a 6 pound bottle, the wine itself may be worth less than 1 pound. Fixed costs weigh most on cheap wine.
steps.highlight: Fixed costs weigh on cheap wine

steps.title: Why some wine costs more
steps.body: Higher prices reflect lower yields, hand labour, steep slopes, oak barrels, long ageing and scarcity. Above a certain level, prices follow reputation and demand rather than cost. A Grand Cru Burgundy costs hundreds of pounds because the vineyard is tiny and global demand is high, not because it costs that much to make.
steps.highlight: Cost up to a point, then scarcity

steps.prompt: On a cheap bottle, most of the price is the wine itself.
steps.explanation: Not true. Duty, tax, packaging and margins are fixed or proportional, so on cheap bottles they make up most of the price.

steps.body: Spending a little more often buys a lot more wine. Moving from 6 to 12 pounds can more than triple the value of the liquid in the bottle, since fixed costs stay the same.

steps.prompt: What mainly drives the price of the most expensive wines?
steps.explanation: At the top, prices follow reputation, scarcity and demand.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Price includes grapes, making, packaging, duty, tax and margins
Fixed costs dominate the price of cheap wine
Top prices follow scarcity and demand
